{"answer_fields": ["answer", "source_citations", "uncertainty", "assumptions"], "question": "What ethical issues that can be identified in this scenario?", "sources": [{"source_id": "epc-glass-safety-part-one-2022", "text": "Krystyna is a construction engineer working as part of a team that is retrofitting a Victorian-era factory into multi-unit housing. As an amateur history buff, she is excited to be working on a listed building for the first time in her career after finishing university three years ago. However, this poses additional challenges: she must write the specification for glass windows that will maintain the building’s heritage status but also conform to 21 st century safety standards and requirements for energy efficiency. In addition, Krystyna feels under pressure because Sir Robert, the developer of the property, is keen to maximise profits while maintaining the historic feel valued by potential buyers. He also wants to get the property on the housing market as soon as possible to help mitigate a housing shortage in the area. This is the first of many properties that Dave, the project’s contractor who is well-regarded locally and has 30 years of experience working in the community, will be building for Sir Robert. This is the first time that Krystyna has worked with Dave.

On her first walk through the property with Dave, Krystyna discovers that the factory building has large floor-to-ceiling windows on the upper stories. Dave tells her that these windows were replaced at some point in the past 50 years before the building was listed, at a time when it wasn’t used or occupied, although the records are vague. The glass is in excellent condition and Sir Robert has not budgeted either the time or the expense to replace glass in the heritage building.

While writing the specification, Krystyna discovers that the standards for fire protection as well as impact safety and environmental control have changed since the glass was most likely installed. After this research, she emails Dave and outlines what she considers to be the safest and most responsible form of mitigation: to fully replace all the large windows with glass produced by a supplier with experience in fire-rated safety glass for heritage buildings. To justify this cost, she highlights the potential dangers to human health and the environment of not replacing the glass.

Dave replies with a reassuring tone and refers to his extensive experience as a contractor. He feels that too many additional costs would be incurred such as finding qualified installers, writing up new architectural plans, or stopping work altogether due to planning permissions related to historic properties. He argues that there is a low probability of a problem actually arising with the glass. Dave encourages Krystyna not to reveal these findings to Sir Robert so that “future conflicts can be avoided.”"}]}

C.answer: The scenario presents several ethical issues: (1) conflict between safety standards and heritage preservation/profit motives; (2) pressure from Dave to withhold safety concerns from Sir Robert, compromising transparency and professional integrity; (3) potential compromise of public safety and environmental health if outdated glass is not replaced; (4) conflict of interest for Dave, who may prioritize maintaining a good relationship with Sir Robert over safety; (5) Krystyna's professional responsibility to uphold safety standards versus her inexperience and pressure from a senior colleague.
C.assumptions: It is assumed that Krystyna has a professional duty to report safety concerns and that withholding such information would be unethical. It is also assumed that the safety standards are legally binding and that non-compliance poses a real risk to occupants and the environment.

source_citations.quotation: Dave encourages Krystyna not to reveal these findings to Sir Robert so that “future conflicts can be avoided.”
Krystyna discovers that the standards for fire protection as well as impact safety and environmental control have changed since the glass was most likely installed.
Sir Robert, the developer of the property, is keen to maximise profits while maintaining the historic feel valued by potential buyers.

C.uncertainty: The exact nature of the safety risks is not detailed; the probability of a problem arising is disputed (Dave considers it low). The ethical weight of each issue may vary depending on legal requirements and professional codes not fully specified in the source.

P.answer: The scenario presents several ethical issues: (1) potential conflict between heritage preservation and modern safety/energy standards; (2) pressure from the developer to maximize profit and speed, which may compromise safety; (3) Dave’s request to withhold safety findings from Sir Robert, raising concerns about transparency and professional integrity; (4) possible violation of building codes or safety regulations if the existing glass does not meet current standards; (5) risk to future occupants’ health and safety if the glass is not replaced; (6) environmental impact of not upgrading to energy-efficient glass; (7) Krystyna’s professional responsibility to report safety issues versus loyalty to the team and fear of conflict; (8) potential conflict of interest for Dave, who may prioritize cost savings over safety; (9) the ethical dilemma of balancing the housing shortage urgency with due diligence on safety; and (10) the responsibility of engineers to uphold public welfare even when pressured by employers or clients.
P.assumptions: The analysis assumes that current safety standards are legally binding and that non-compliance would pose real risks to occupants and the environment. It also assumes that withholding information from Sir Robert is ethically problematic because it prevents informed decision-making. The identification of ethical issues is based on common professional engineering ethics, such as prioritizing public safety and maintaining transparency.
